title: Will Iran Turn Into a Forever War? | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Ray Takeyh argues the U.S. war in Iran launched in February is repeating the McNamara-era doctrine of gradual escalation that failed in Vietnam: killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei did not break the theocracy, and Iran's counter-leverage is imposing costs on global commerce through the Persian Gulf. He expects a strike-counterstrike spiral toward significant American casualties and a humanitarian crisis, and argues the only exit — a UN-authorized multinational escort force — will in practice fall disproportionately on the U.S. Navy.

themes.theme: Gradual escalation as a doctrine with a failing record

insights.claim: The doctrine of calibrated incremental military escalation was developed in the 1960s by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara and his Pentagon 'whiz kids' on the theory that mounting pressure would make an adversary conclude the war's costs exceeded its benefits and then negotiate on Washington's terms.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Recognizing the escalation playbook in advance lets you forecast the sequence of U.S. actions rather than react to each strike as news.
insights.quote: This idea of incremental escalation was first developed in the 1960s by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara and his so-called whiz kids in the Pentagon—often PhDs with impressive credentials but little common sense.
insights.locator: This idea of incremental escalation was first developed

insights.claim: Coercive escalation fails because it discounts an enemy's capacity to absorb punishment and adapt: bombing campaigns fortify leaders' will, galvanize the population behind resistance, and prompt the adversary to match escalation with escalation, steadily widening the conflict.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Escalation is a widening rather than a terminating mechanism, so risk models should assume conflict expansion, not resolution, after each strike round.
insights.quote: Bombing campaigns fortify the will of the leaders and often galvanize the population behind the cause of resistance.
insights.locator: The problem with this kind of approach

insights.claim: In Vietnam the escalation strategy led America to drop more bombs than in all its previous wars combined on a country slightly larger than New Mexico, with roughly three million Vietnamese dead.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: The historical benchmark for how far gradual escalation runs before it stops — orders of magnitude beyond what markets typically price as a 'limited' campaign.
insights.quote: In Vietnam, this strategy ultimately led America to drop more bombs than it had in all its previous wars combined on a country slightly larger than New Mexico, with a staggering casualty figure of approximately three million dead Vietnamese.
insights.locator: In Vietnam, this strategy ultimately led America

themes.theme: Why the Iran war began and why the regime held

insights.claim: It remains unclear why President Trump launched the war in Iran in February, because the administration's explanations have shifted and the stated objectives have constantly moved.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Undefined war aims mean no observable off-ramp, which raises the duration premium on any Middle East risk exposure.
insights.quote: The administration’s explanations have shifted and the goalpost has constantly moved.
insights.locator: It is still not entirely clear why President Trump

insights.claim: Two January events — a successful operation in Venezuela that removed President Nicolás Maduro and an uprising in Iran that shook the regime's foundations — appear to have convinced Trump he could score an easy victory in the Middle East, a misreading because the Islamic Republic proved vicious enough to restore order and has deeper roots in society than a Latin American kleptocracy.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Extrapolating regime-change success from Venezuela to Iran is the analytical error at the root of the war — a warning against reading one autocracy's fragility into another's.
insights.quote: But this was a misreading of Iran’s politics as the Islamic Republic was vicious enough to restore order and has deeper roots in the society than a Latin American kleptocracy.
insights.locator: First, there was a successful operation in Venezuela

insights.claim: America and Israel opened the war by killing scores of Iranian officials including the elderly Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, yet the system held and the theocracy's multilayered elite maintained control, with the reconstituted regime treating the conflict as a life-or-death struggle.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Decapitation of the Iranian leadership has already been tried and failed — the decapitation-ends-the-war scenario should be removed from base cases.
insights.quote: But the system held, and the theocracy’s multilayered elite maintained control.
insights.locator: America, joined by Israel, began the war

themes.theme: Hormuz leverage and the contest of wills

insights.claim: Iran's indispensable source of leverage is its ability to impose costs on the global economy and American taxpayers by taking the fight into the Persian Gulf, mauling America's regional allies and disrupting maritime traffic through critical waterways.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Iran's escalation instrument is economic and maritime, so tanker rates, war-risk insurance and Gulf shipping volumes are the live transmission channel to global markets.
insights.quote: This was Iran’s indispensable source of leverage: It could impose costs on the global economy and American taxpayers alike.
insights.locator: The reconstituted regime viewed the conflict as a life-or-death struggle

insights.claim: In a coercive contest the decisive variable is not who can inflict more pain but who is prepared to endure more, and a party that views the struggle in existential terms has a greater incentive to absorb punishment than a distant empire waging a war of choice.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Asymmetric pain tolerance favors Iran in a long war, implying the conflict resolves on Tehran's timeline rather than Washington's.
insights.quote: The question is not who can inflict more pain, but who is prepared to endure more.
insights.locator: This was Iran’s indispensable source of leverage

insights.claim: Trump's strategy is defined by unpredictability, with military campaigns repeatedly called off and then quickly resumed, yet it still follows the logic of gradual escalation — he publicly pledged that every time Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz the United States will destroy one bridge or power plant, including targets in or next to Tehran.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: An explicit, publicly stated tit-for-tat rule makes escalation mechanically predictable: each shipping incident now carries a pre-announced strike on Iranian infrastructure.
insights.quote: From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT
insights.locator: Unpredictability appears to be the defining feature

insights.claim: Iranians are already enduring power outages, food shortages, and debilitating inflation and unemployment, meaning further infrastructure strikes land on a population already in economic distress.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Domestic Iranian hardship has not produced capitulation, undercutting the assumption that economic pain forces political concessions.
insights.quote: The Iranian people are already suffering from power outages, food shortages, and debilitating inflation and unemployment rates.
insights.locator: The Iranian people are already suffering

insights.claim: Iran is likely to answer further attacks on its territory by striking U.S. military installations across the region and potentially inflicting significant American casualties, which would provoke retaliation and set off a cycle of strikes and counterstrikes with an ever-expanding target list.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: American casualties in the region are the specific catalyst that would force a step-change in U.S. commitment and in oil and defense pricing.
insights.quote: Given the stakes, Iran is likely to respond to further attacks on its territory by striking US military installations across the region, potentially inflicting significant American casualties.
insights.locator: Given the stakes, Iran is likely to respond

insights.claim: The longer the war continues the more likely the distinction between civilian and military targets erodes, which is how humanitarian crises unfold — one step at a time.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Duration itself, not any single decision, is the driver of the worst outcomes — time is the risk variable to track.
insights.quote: This is how humanitarian crises unfold—one step at a time.
insights.locator: The longer the war goes on

themes.theme: Freedom of navigation and who pays for it

insights.claim: Because freedom of navigation is a core principle of the rules-based international order and the Persian Gulf is critical to global commerce, the United States should appeal to the United Nations to authorize a multinational force dedicated to ensuring safe passage of all ships through the Gulf.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: A UN-authorized escort mission is the identifiable de-escalation path; movement at the Security Council would be the signal that Gulf shipping risk is peaking.
insights.quote: A core principle of the rules-based international order is the freedom of navigation.
insights.locator: The Persian Gulf is an international waterway

insights.claim: Given the Trump administration's skepticism toward alliances and multilateral institutions, securing international authorization will be difficult, and whatever sanction is granted the burden of ensuring free passage through the Gulf will fall disproportionately on the U.S. Navy for the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: An open-ended U.S. naval escort commitment implies sustained defense outlays and a persistent Gulf risk premium regardless of any diplomatic settlement.
insights.quote: the burden of ensuring free passage through the Gulf will fall disproportionately on the U.S. Navy for the foreseeable future
insights.locator: Given the Trump administration’s skepticism toward alliances

insights.claim: Unwise wars launched without sufficient deliberation produce consequences long after their authors leave power, as George Ball warned Lyndon Johnson in 1964 that once on the tiger's back one cannot be sure of picking the place to dismount.
insights.speaker: Ray Takeyh
insights.so_what: Frames the Iran war as a multi-administration commitment rather than an election-cycle event — the exit is not controlled by whoever started it.
insights.quote: Once on the tiger’s back, we cannot be sure of picking the place to dismount.
insights.locator: Unwise wars launched without sufficient deliberation
